common_name: Vanessa Grape (Cold-Hardy Canadian Seedless Red Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; very cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Vanessa was bred in Ontario, Canada, for cold hardiness and reliable production of seedless red table grapes even in shorter, cooler growing seasons than many seedless varieties tolerate. The medium-sized, crisp, firm berries carry a bright, sweet, well-balanced flavor and hold well on the vine without splitting, making them good for fresh eating straight off the vine as well as for juice. The vigorous, productive vine is a solid choice for northern home gardens wanting a genuinely good-tasting seedless grape without relying on less cold-hardy varieties bred for milder climates. Train to a permanent trellis system, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size and flavor.

common_name: Mars Grape (Disease-Resistant Southern Seedless Blue Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; bred at the University of Arkansas for disease resistance and good performance in warm, humid Southern climates, well adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Mars was bred at the University of Arkansas specifically for good disease resistance and reliable performance in the warm, humid Southern climates where many other seedless table grapes struggle with fungal disease pressure, combining that practical resilience with sweet, blue-black, seedless berries carrying a mild, classic grape flavor. The compact, manageable vine is well suited to home garden trellises and arbors, and its combination of hardiness and disease tolerance has made it one of the more dependable seedless grape choices for Southern home gardeners. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter to control vigor, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size.

common_name: Einset Seedless Grape (Strawberry-Flavored Cornell Red Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Einset Seedless was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York research station, producing small to medium, pink-red, seedless berries with a distinctive, delicately fruity flavor often described as reminiscent of strawberry, an unusual and pleasant trait that sets it apart from more neutrally flavored table grapes. The vine is cold-hardy and ripens relatively early in the season, giving gardeners in shorter-season regions a good chance at a full seedless grape harvest before fall frost. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if the vine sets a heavy crop, since concentrated clusters develop better size and flavor than overcrowded ones.

common_name: Somerset Seedless Grape (Extremely Cold-Hardy Spicy-Sweet Red Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; exceptionally cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 3-7.

directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Somerset Seedless was bred by pioneering grape breeder Elmer Swenson in Wisconsin, developed for extreme cold hardiness that lets it survive winters far too harsh for most table grapes, while still producing small, red, seedless berries with a sweet flavor carrying a distinctive light spiciness reminiscent of some native American grape species in its parentage. This combination of genuine cold hardiness and good eating quality has made it one of the standard recommendations for far-northern home gardeners wanting a real seedless grape harvest. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size.

common_name: Swenson Red Grape (Cold-Hardy Northern Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; very cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 4-7.

directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Swenson Red is another cold-hardy northern grape developed by breeder Elmer Swenson in Wisconsin, producing medium, pinkish-red table grapes with sweet, richly flavored flesh and a tender skin, considered by many Northern growers to be one of the best-tasting hardy grapes available, even though it retains seeds unlike some of Swenson's later seedless introductions. The vigorous vine is a reliable producer in climates too cold for most vinifera or Southern-bred hybrid grapes, extending quality fresh grape growing well into regions with harsh winters. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if the vine sets a heavy crop for the best berry size and flavor.
